title: One rule for every class-init request waits on its own thread, and TLC finds the deadlock
summary: A request for a class being initialized waits, unless it comes from the initializing thread itself, which is a recursive request and completes normally (step 3 of JVMS §5.5). A developer removes the exception: every request during initialization waits, one rule, and the lock serializes everything. The contract diff is one line and is approved. The model checker, with deadlock detection on, finds a five-step run after which no thread can move: the initializer touched its own class, waited for itself, and every other thread waits for it.

change.description: In state `IN_PROGRESS`, answer `WAIT` to every request, the initializing thread's included. The reasoning: a class is not usable until its initializer has returned, and the special case for the initializing thread was a way of not holding the lock across `<clinit>`, which the lock release already provides. The behavioural contract is regenerated and its diff is one line, the case `decide(IN_PROGRESS, Request[byInitializingThread=true])`, `PROCEED` to `WAIT`; the test for that case is updated. The reviewer approves the diff.

risk: A class initializer that refers to its own class is ordinary Java: a static field initialized by a static method of the same class, an enum whose constants are built in `<clinit>` and call a static helper, a singleton whose constructor reads a static. Each of these is a request for the class by the thread that is initializing it, and step 3 exists so that it completes. With this change the thread waits for an initialization only it can finish, and every thread that needs the class afterwards waits behind it: a JVM that hangs on the first enum it loads, with no exception and a thread dump that shows every thread waiting in class initialization. The invariants of the model all hold, because nothing wrong is ever observed; the failure is that nothing is observed at all, which is what deadlock detection is for. The contract diff could not catch this: the diff was precisely the intended change.
explanation: The TLA+ model has one action per operation of a thread, with the runtime's decision rule generated from the behavioural contract of `ClassInitialization#decide`, which the tool proves the bytecode satisfies on all 30 inputs. TLC is run with deadlock checking: a reachable state in which no action is enabled is reported, except the one in which every thread is done, which the model marks as its end. It reports the shortest run: one thread requests the class and starts the initializer; the initializer touches its own class and the thread is told to wait; the two other threads request the class and are told to wait. Five steps, the initial state and four actions, and then no thread can move: the initializer is waiting for a completion that only it could produce. The unpatched rule passes the same check in 37 states, which is the proof that step 3 is what prevents it.
resolution: Revert. Step 3 is not an optimisation of the locking; it is the definition of a recursive request, and the JLS makes the same exception in §12.4.2 for the same reason. If the developer wants one rule, it is "a request by the initializing thread proceeds, any other waits", which is the two cases of the contract as they were. Deadlock checking stays on in the model's build so that the next change to the rule is checked for it.
provenance: Constructed from step 3 of the initialization procedure of JVMS §5.5, by removing it.
